title: DiveDex
subtitle: Real-time Marine Recognition System for Recreational Divers
intro: A hybrid system combining smart diving goggles with real-time marine species recognition and a companion mobile app that records and visualizes the fish encountered during a dive.

steps.description: Dual fisheye cameras on each wrist capture 120fps video of both divers’ hands without bulky housings.
TensorFlow.js runs on an onboard Jetson Nano, comparing the gesture to a library of 60 baseline signals plus any custom packs the buddy team added.
A color-coded HUD flashes the translation, vibrates the relevant finger, and saves the signal + depth data to a dive log you can review on shore.

images.caption: Low-fidelity prototype showing paired HUDs, mobile prep app, and gesture history.

title: Labyrinth
subtitle: A two-player asymmetric hide-and-seek game in the dark
intro: A two-player asymmetric hide-and-seek game set in a dark maze. One player becomes the Hider (a living person trying to escape), while the other becomes the Seeker (a ghostly entity that hunts through sound).

meta.role: Game design, Physical Computation, Visual Design

sections.title: Concept
sections.body: Labyrinth is an asymmetric two-player game about perception. Player 1 navigates a maze using Leap Motion as an Arduino-driven light input that reveals a cone of vision in-game. Player 2 cannot see the maze; instead, they track the hider through spatialized footsteps, inspired by echolocation. The tension comes from incomplete, unequal senses—light versus echo.

sections.alt: Screenshot of the dark maze environment
sections.caption: Each player's experience of the maze is distinct—vision vs. hearing.

sections.title: Research
sections.body: The game began as a study of sensory asymmetry in cooperative and competitive play. References included horror sound design and echo-based mechanics like those in *Dark Echo*. We explored how withholding one sense amplifies another and how players communicate under unequal perception.

images.caption: Early prototype built in Unity showing light cone rendering.
Final two-player setup: Leap Motion for the hider, headphones for the seeker.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: The final version emphasizes the emotional contrast between panic and patience. The Hider experiences claustrophobic flashes of visibility; the Seeker, drifting through echo, becomes both blind and omnipresent. The piece explores how unequal information defines empathy, fear, and control in play.

title: Spinphony
subtitle: A record-player platformer steered by a tangible controller
intro: A playful Unity platformer where a lost musical note (Do) spins through rhythm puzzles using a custom-built turntable controller with arcade buttons.

meta.role: Game design, Hardware prototyping, Visual design

sections.title: Concept
sections.body: Spinphony treats the turntable as both controller and narrative device. Rotating the platter spins Do, a lost note, through looping levels of rhythm gates and percussive enemies. Two arcade buttons act as jump and dash, so the player's whole body performs tiny DJ gestures to keep the character on beat.

sections.alt: Custom Spinphony controller and Unity build
sections.caption: Final hardware build: laser-cut platter, rotary encoder, and arcade buttons feeding a Unity platformer.

steps.description: Breadboarded an Arduino-based rotary encoder and tuned the resolution so one full spin maps to a comfortable in-game speed without motion sickness.
Unity interprets encoder delta as horizontal velocity, while button combinations trigger vaults, slides, and tempo boosts synchronized to the soundtrack.
Illustrated bold shapes inspired by vinyl sleeves and animated parallax backgrounds to reinforce the feeling of traveling through grooves.

images.caption: Early block-out level used to calibrate encoder sensitivity.
Final character art and rhythm obstacles.
Unity view showing layered parallax backgrounds.
Custom UI referencing vinyl liner notes.
Playtesting session with full controller setup.

sections.title: Playthrough
sections.caption: The turntable controller driving the Unity build.

sections.title: What I learned
sections.body: Framing the controller as an instrument kept playtesters focused on rhythm rather than button combos. I learned how much onboarding clarity matters for tangible interfaces and how to choreograph UI feedback—lights, vibrations, and animation—so players always know what the controller is asking them to do.

title: Chester Choiceworth
subtitle: "You don't choose your lifestyle. Data does."
intro: An interactive installation that turns your spending habits into an experience. You upload your own transaction history, and the system prints targeted lifestyle ads back at you.

sections.title: What is Chester Choiceworth?
sections.body: Chester Choiceworth is an interactive installation that turns your spending habits into a playful but slightly uncomfortable mirror. By uploading your monthly transaction record, the system generates two things: (1) a digital receipt summarizing what you spent and where, and (2) a stream of targeted 'lifestyle suggestions' printed on a physical receipt printer. The tone is fake-friendly, like a personal financial assistant that thinks it knows who you are and what kind of life you deserve.

sections.alt: Physical installation of the Chester Choiceworth setup with printer and display
sections.caption: The installation in use: live dashboard + receipt printer quietly judging you.

sections.title: Why I made this
sections.body: We like to believe that lifestyle is about taste, identity, and choice. But in practice, a lot of what gets sold back to us is inferred from our transaction history. What you buy predicts what tier you 'belong to' — grocery store loyalty cards, rent size, Uber vs subway, Whole Foods vs dollar slice. Chester Choiceworth exaggerates that logic out loud. It behaves like a marketing engine that decides: are you luxury-coded, survival-coded, guilty, aspirational, or failing?

sections.title: How it presents you back to yourself

images.caption: Spending map generated from your uploaded transactions: where your money actually goes in the city.
Auto-generated summary receipt: categories, totals, and 'lifestyle grade'.
Thermal printer output: targeted ads and financial advice written in a manipulative 'personalized concierge' voice.

steps.description: User uploads a JSON of their monthly transactions (date, vendor, price, category).
Node.js script groups spending by category (rent, groceries, snacks, transport, etc.) and estimates relative financial pressure, e.g. % of income spent on rent.
The browser shows a live dashboard: a map of where you spent, and a printed-like digital 'receipt' of totals.
Arduino + thermal printer spits out exaggerated 'ads' for either budget survival items or high-end lifestyle products, depending on what you 'look like' to the system.

sections.title: Tone / Concept
sections.body: The piece is intentionally condescending. It's a parody of recommendation systems. If your rent is 60% of your spending, it might suggest: 'You seem stressed. Consider a Bentley leather sofa to elevate your relaxation tier.' If you eat instant noodles and bodega snacks, it might message you like you're a cost-optimization problem. The joke is that personalization becomes class surveillance dressed as help.

sections.title: Demo Clip
sections.caption: Live capture of the loop: upload → analyze → map → insult.

sections.title: What I learned / next steps
sections.body: People loved seeing the spend map, but reacted strongest to the printer. Physical paper felt like a 'verdict'. The next iteration will generate different styles of printed output depending on the audience — for example: landlord report, bank report, partner report — to show how different entities read the same data and judge you differently.

title: Marbility
subtitle: How to Show Off Quantum Computing
intro: An experimental physics-based gameplay exploring how to visualize the logic of quantum computing through marbles and motion.

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
This interactive exhibit introduces the audience to quantum concepts of entanglement, gates, probability, and qubits through an interactive game.

In the game, you and your teammate each control a qubit and try to score the correct probability given to you. You interact with gates and learn about probability and entanglement. With the aesthetics of Pinball and Plinko–widely-known, nostalgic games that are easy to understand–we attract people of all ages and backgrounds.

Inspired by old arcade games such as Plinko and Pinball.

sections.title: How to Play
sections.body:
1. This is a 2-player game—bring a friend and play on the same team!

2. Press the Start button on the right to launch the round.

3. Both players receive a probability target while a countdown begins.

4. Each player applies single-qubit gates using their side of the board; rotating the encoder knob sends an Rx gate to evolve the qubit state.

5. Ten levers on each board affect the shared superposition. Some move independently, while entangled levers mirror or invert the teammate's motion, so one player's gate can change the other's qubit.

6. Hitting the large Entangle button reshuffles the entanglement graph, reassigning which levers link and how strongly they influence each other.

7. Tap your personal X-gate button to flip your qubit instantly when timing matters.

8. When the countdown hits zero, all inputs freeze and players pour marbles into the top of the machine.

9. Marbles cascade through the boards and get tallied at the base.

10. Once every marble is counted, the scoreboard reveals each player's accuracy and the final team score.
